opeds.headline: Stop Arguing About AI's Soul. Look at the Water Bill.
opeds.subtitle: The tech industry's grand utopian and apocalyptic narratives are just marketing tactics designed to hide the mundane theft of public resources and personal privacy.
opeds.body:
While Silicon Valley preaches techno-salvation and Washington panics over science-fiction apocalypses, the actual machines are busy draining rural aquifers and quietly vacuuming up our private lives to pad a few balance sheets. We are treated to a relentless theatrical production where the only two permitted characters are a utopian savior and a digital grim reaper. Both roles are played by the exact same people, and both serve the exact same purpose: distracting you from the heavy iron, concrete, and copper being laid down right now to lock in corporate rent-extraction.

Here is what that looks like on the ground. There is a data center cooling tower humming in a small Iowa town right now, chewing through millions of gallons of local drinking water while the city council gets promised vague high-tech jobs that never quite materialize. There is an auxiliary-data broker selling your personal digital exhaust to training pipelines before any software model even boots up. The high-minded safety debates in congressional hearing rooms obsess over whether an autonomous agent might eventually outsmart its creators. Meanwhile, the actual robbery is happening upstream at the data-broker layer, where your life history is repackaged and priced as a commodity without your consent.

We keep inventing elaborate fantasy frameworks to govern this technology, as if we are dealing with a visitation from the cosmos rather than an industrial project run by standard-issue utility monopolies. Solvency mechanisms like insurance pools and corporate compliance floors answer who pays after a disaster strikes, but they leave the core standard of care entirely untouched. They give a boardroom lawyer a checklist to initial while the underlying extraction of privacy and public resources accelerates unchecked. Pinning liability to a named corporate officer on a compliance sheet is fine theater, but it misses the baseline reality that the entire architecture is built on non-consensual data harvesting. You cannot regulate away the fundamental theft of human attention with a few extra lines in an enterprise compliance manual.

Algorithmic disgorgement offers a brief flash of what actual accountability could look like when regulators force companies to burn down models trained on stolen private records. Yet even those rare punitive settlements get treated as dramatic exceptions rather than the baseline rule they should be. The tech barons want you to believe their systems are too vast, too complex, and too mysterious to be held to ordinary laws of physics, economics, and common decency. They want you lost in the fog of existential speculation so you never look at the local energy grid straining to power their server farms or the exploited labor sorting toxic training data behind closed doors.

If this massive infrastructure project were truly about human liberation, why are the profits privatized while the water, the electricity, and the privacy costs are socialized onto everyone else? Who gave these corporations the deed to our collective digital history, and why are we letting them hide behind fairy tales about artificial minds while they build a very ordinary, very profitable tollbooth on human communication?

opeds.rhetorical_meta: This piece deploys a demystifying materialist strategy, stripping away abstract speculative jargon about existential risk and replacing it with concrete physical realities like water consumption and data brokers. By framing the entire AI debate as an elaborate distraction masking standard corporate rent-extraction, the prose forces the reader to confront the immediate economic and infrastructural costs borne by everyday people.
